forces.title: Global electronics supply chain shifting due to geopolitics, resilience, regulation
forces.description: The global electronics supply chain is undergoing a fundamental transformation, moving away from a cost-optimized, China-centric model. Geopolitical tensions, the need for supply chain resilience highlighted by the 2021-22 semiconductor shortage, and regulatory pressures like the US/EU CHIPS Acts and India's PLI schemes are driving diversification. This creates new opportunities for alternative manufacturing hubs and impacts the sourcing strategy for critical components like semiconductors.

forces.title: India's EMS "scale without depth" due to import reliance
forces.description: India's Electronic Manufacturing Services (EMS) sector, while growing rapidly in mobile assembly, exhibits "scale without depth." This means a heavy reliance on imported components, including semiconductors, displays, and PCBs, which constitute 60-90% of the bill of materials. This structural vulnerability limits domestic value addition and margin retention, preventing India from moving up the value chain to higher-complexity segments like automotive or industrial electronics.

forces.title: Drive to localize electronics value chain for higher value capture
forces.description: India's EMS sector is currently heavily reliant on imported electronic components, including semiconductors, limiting domestic value addition. There is a strong imperative and emerging opportunity for Indian EMS players to localize the supply chain, build engineering depth, supply chain sophistication, and manage OEM relationships at the design stage. This evolution from basic assembly to integration and localization is crucial for mitigating forex risks, import duties, supply volatility, and capturing higher value in the electronics sector.

forces.title: Heavy reliance on imported components for electronics manufacturing
forces.description: India's rapidly growing Electronics Manufacturing Services (EMS) industry is structurally constrained by its heavy reliance on imported components, including semiconductors, displays, and PCBs. Unlike mature ecosystems, India lacks a deep domestic supply chain for these critical inputs, forcing EMS players to depend on long-haul imports. This results in high embedded import content in final products, limiting domestic value capture and exposing the sector to supply chain vulnerabilities, higher working capital needs, and cost competitiveness issues.

forces.title: Lower productivity and higher costs compared to global EMS hubs
forces.description: Despite a large labor pool, India's Electronics Manufacturing Services (EMS) sector faces productivity gaps compared to established hubs like China and Vietnam. These gaps stem from lower automation density, limited exposure to complex manufacturing processes, and inconsistent availability of skilled technicians. Combined with higher working capital due to long import lead times, NPI agility issues, and additional costs from import duties and freight on heavily imported components (60-90% of BOM), India's cost competitiveness is partially offset, limiting domestic value-add and margin retention.

forces.title: Government-led strategic push for semiconductor indigenization
forces.description: The India Semiconductor Mission is a pivotal government policy initiative, strategically committing to component-level indigenization. Approved investments in domestic fabrication plants and Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) facilities are set to significantly reduce India's near-total import dependence for semiconductors. This mission acts as a powerful tailwind for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector by directly stimulating demand for advanced machinery and specialized materials required for chip manufacturing and packaging within the country.

forces.title: Over-reliance on incentives creating competitive dependence
forces.description: The current policy framework, while effective in stimulating capacity, risks creating an "incentive-led plateau" for India's electronics manufacturing sector, including semiconductor production. If cost competitiveness remains structurally dependent on Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) disbursements rather than intrinsic productivity and ecosystem advantages, the industry faces a viability cliff as these incentive cycles conclude. This dependence could undermine long-term, sustainable growth and deter the development of genuine competitive capabilities for semiconductor equipment and materials.

forces.title: Policy must shift to capability incentives for sustained competitiveness
forces.description: To ensure durable growth and genuine competitiveness in India's electronics and semiconductor sectors, policy design must evolve beyond mere capacity-building incentives. The next phase needs to prioritize "capability incentives," specifically rewarding domestic value-add intensity, the attainment of critical certifications, and deeper design integration. This shift is crucial to foster a robust ecosystem for semiconductor equipment and materials, moving away from an over-reliance on financial disbursements and towards nurturing inherent productivity and innovation.

forces.title: India's R&D investment lags global leaders in electronics
forces.description: India's Gross Expenditure on Research and Development (GERD) stands at only 0.6-0.7% of GDP, significantly lower than leading countries (e.g., 2.4%). Private-sector participation in electronics R&D is also markedly lower than in the US, China, and South Korea. This underinvestment in R&D, particularly in advanced areas like EUV lithography and precision etching crucial for semiconductor nodes (5nm to 3nm), poses a direct headwind for the advancement and indigenization of semiconductor equipment and materials technology in India.

forces.title: Fragmented electronics supply base hinders cost efficiency, scaling
forces.description: India's electronics supply base is characterized by fragmentation and a thin presence of Tier-2 and Tier-3 suppliers. This contrasts sharply with clustered ecosystems found in China and Japan, which enable scale and cost efficiency. The absence of such integrated industrial clusters limits the ability of domestic manufacturers, including potential semiconductor equipment and materials producers, to achieve cost compression, rapid scaling, and reliable upstream sourcing, thereby impeding the growth of a comprehensive electronics manufacturing ecosystem.

forces.title: Global nations' strategies offer roadmap for India's semiconductor growth
forces.description: Lessons from leading nations like Japan, China, and South Korea provide a clear roadmap for India's ambition in semiconductors. Their success was built on focused industrial policies, early movement into higher-value segments like semiconductors and components, establishing industrial clusters, and significant investments in R&D, including public co-financing for advanced fabrication and packaging facilities. These strategies underscore the importance of sustained, coordinated efforts that would profoundly benefit India's Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector.

forces.title: Strategic focus on R&D and component manufacturing
forces.description: India's priority actions to boost electronics competitiveness include scaling R&D investment and strengthening in-house design capabilities to reduce import dependence. A parallel push to deepen component manufacturing, supported by stronger MSME participation, is aimed at significantly enhancing domestic value addition. These initiatives are direct tailwinds for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector, as they seek to establish a more integrated domestic ecosystem where advanced design and manufacturing capabilities drive demand for specialized equipment and materials.

forces.title: Booming AI and DeepTech sectors driving demand for advanced chips
forces.description: The rapid expansion of India's AI market, projected to reach US$131.31 billion by 2032 with a 42.2% CAGR, coupled with the DeepTech sector's forecast 2.5-fold growth, represents a significant tailwind for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials industry. AI requires increasingly powerful and specialized chips, driving demand for advanced semiconductor design and fabrication. This translates directly into higher demand for the sophisticated equipment and materials necessary to produce these cutting-edge semiconductors, underpinning long-term growth for the sector.

forces.title: Significant government investment in semiconductor equipment and materials
forces.description: The Union Budget 2026–27 launched the India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 (ISM 2.0) with a substantial outlay of Rs. 8,000 crore (US$ 0.90 billion) for FY27, specifically targeting the development of domestic capabilities in semiconductor equipment and materials. This, alongside the Prime Minister laying the foundation for three semiconductor plants with over US$15 billion investment, indicates a strong government commitment. These initiatives directly drive demand and foster a conducive environment for the IN080402 sector.

forces.title: Private sector investments in semiconductor manufacturing & packaging
forces.description: Tata Electronics' memorandum of understanding with Intel to explore semiconductor manufacturing and advanced packaging in India signals significant private sector investment in the sector. Plans include an OSAT facility in Assam by 2026 and a foundry in Dholera, Gujarat, by mid-2027, along with collaborations on AI-focused computing solutions. These private ventures, supported by government schemes, are direct drivers for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector by creating new domestic production capacities requiring advanced machinery and materials.

forces.title: Commencement of commercial production by new semiconductor units
forces.description: The announcement that four semiconductor units will commence commercial production in 2026 is a significant tailwind for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector. This direct expansion of manufacturing capacity within India creates immediate demand for advanced lithography, deposition, etch, metrology, and packaging/test equipment, as well as essential materials like silicon wafers and photoresists. It validates the government's strategic initiatives and marks a tangible step towards domestic semiconductor ecosystem growth.

forces.title: Government schemes supporting semiconductor startups and design
forces.description: The Design Linked Incentive (DLI) Scheme, which supports 24 semiconductor design startups and has attracted nearly Rs. 430 crore (US$ 0.05 billion) in venture funding, is a tailwind for India's semiconductor ecosystem. Although focused on design (IN080401), a thriving design community, particularly supported by government initiatives, directly implies future demand for fabrication services and, by extension, the equipment and materials (including EDA software) needed to bring these designs to production.

forces.title: National Policy on Electronics promoting chipset manufacturing
forces.description: The National Policy on Electronics (NPE) 2019 is a significant tailwind, envisioning India as a global hub for Electronics System Design & Manufacturing (ESDM). A core objective is to encourage and drive capabilities for developing core components, particularly chipsets. This strategic focus directly translates into increased demand for semiconductor equipment and materials as domestic chipset manufacturing scales up, creating a more robust and self-reliant ecosystem for advanced electronics production in India.

forces.title: 5G and IoT adoption fuels demand for electronics, semiconductors
forces.description: Technology transitions such as the rollout of 5G networks and the proliferation of IoT (Internet of Things) devices are significantly accelerating the adoption of electronic products. These advanced technologies require sophisticated and high-performance semiconductors for connectivity, processing, and sensing. This growing demand for underlying electronic components acts as a strong tailwind for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector, as it necessitates increased production capacity and advanced manufacturing capabilities for chips.

forces.title: Increased M&A and investment in chip design capabilities
forces.description: The surge in M&A activity within the tech sector, including Infosys's acquisition of semiconductor design firm InSemi, signals growing investment in India's chip design capabilities. Such acquisitions expand crucial skills in areas like chip design (IN080401) and contribute to developing a more robust domestic semiconductor ecosystem. A stronger design foundation inevitably drives demand for sophisticated EDA software, which is classified under Semiconductor Equipment & Materials (IN080402), making this a key upside driver for the sector.

forces.title: Global tech firms investing in India's semiconductor R&D and manufacturing
forces.description: Major global technology firms like LG Electronics and Samsung Electronics are increasing R&D efforts in India, focusing on semiconductor design, system-on-chip, and AI-enabled technologies, supported by government schemes. Crucially, Foxconn and STMicroelectronics are collaborating to construct a semiconductor plant in India. These direct investments and partnerships by leading international players signal confidence and bring crucial capital, technology, and expertise, significantly bolstering demand and capability development for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector in India.

forces.title: Skill development initiatives for ESDM and semiconductor sector
forces.description: Initiatives by the Electronics Sector Skills Council of India (ESSCI) and India Electronics and Semiconductor Association (IESA) aim to create a world-class, future-ready workforce for the Electronics System Design & Manufacturing (ESDM) sector, including semiconductor design and manufacturing. By bridging academia and industry, these programs address the need for skilled personnel in design, manufacturing, and service, which is critical for the growth and sustained competitiveness of the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials industry in India.

forces.title: Micron's SEZ investment boosts India's semiconductor manufacturing base
forces.description: The approval of Micron Semiconductor's Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Sanand, Gujarat, backed by a US$ 1.51 billion investment, is a significant tailwind for India's Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector. This SEZ is dedicated to semiconductor manufacturing, establishing a crucial facility for chip production. The investment directly translates into demand for sophisticated fabrication equipment and a steady supply of specialized materials required for memory and other chip manufacturing processes, reinforcing India's domestic capabilities.

forces.title: Micron's ATMP facility fuels AI chip assembly, test demand
forces.description: Micron Technology's inauguration of India’s first semiconductor Assembly, Test, Mark, and Pack (ATMP) facility, backed by a US$2.75 billion investment, is a direct and powerful tailwind for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector. This facility specifically targets AI-enabling chips, driving substantial demand for advanced packaging, testing, and R&D equipment and materials. It signifies a crucial step in India's semiconductor value chain, moving beyond just fabrication to include crucial post-fabrication processes domestically.

forces.title: Economic security pacts drive strategic semiconductor development
forces.description: Prime Minister Modi's visit to Japan, securing an economic security pact covering semiconductors, critical minerals, and AI, signifies a strategic international focus on semiconductor supply chain resilience. Such bilateral agreements create a geopolitical imperative and supportive framework for developing domestic semiconductor capabilities. This structural shift encourages investments and policy alignment beneficial for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector, aiming to secure vital inputs and reduce dependence on single geographies.

forces.title: First domestically produced chip by 2025 drives equipment demand
forces.description: India's plan to launch its first domestically produced semiconductor chip by end of 2025, using 28 to 90 nanometre technology, is a powerful tailwind. This initiative is supported by six chip fabrication units under development and the recent approval of a sixth manufacturing facility (HCL and Foxconn JV). The focus on indigenous intellectual property and chip design, targeting sectors like automotive and telecom, directly translates into a strong and immediate demand for the necessary semiconductor equipment and materials for local production.

forces.title: India making "Big Bets" on capital-intensive semiconductor ecosystems
forces.description: India's strategic vision involves making "Big Bets" on capital-intensive, IP-led, and R&D-driven segments like semiconductor ecosystems to drive future value creation. This fundamental shift requires substantial risk capital, intense R&D, coordinated public-private efforts, and sustained policy continuity. For the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector, this represents a structural tailwind as it entails building out advanced manufacturing infrastructure, fostering intellectual property, and investing heavily in the tools and processes essential for state-of-the-art chip fabrication.

forces.title: Public-private partnerships accelerate semiconductor capability building
forces.description: Unlocking India's technological ambition, particularly in semiconductors, requires scaling through structured partnerships. This includes establishing bilateral R&D corridors, fostering regional innovation clusters, and undertaking focused public–private "moonshots" in semiconductors, AI, and deep tech. These collaborative models are crucial for accelerating capability-building, sharing risks, and leveraging collective expertise. For the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector, such partnerships facilitate access to cutting-edge research, infrastructure, and investment, driving innovation and localized development.

forces.title: Greater R&D, startup capital needed for semiconductor innovation
forces.description: To sustain India's global relevance and foster advanced capabilities, there's a strong call for increased investments in R&D and deeper startup risk capital, particularly in areas like semiconductors. This focus aims to transform engineers into inventors and entrepreneurs, driving innovation. For the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector, this represents an upside driver as it would nurture indigenous technological advancements, support the development of specialized tools and materials, and create a more dynamic environment for cutting-edge solutions.

forces.title: Geopolitics, supply chain fragility drive semiconductor onshoring
forces.description: Global macroeconomic uncertainties, marked by geopolitical tensions and supply chain fragility (exacerbated by constrained access to critical inputs like semiconductors), are compelling a significant shift towards onshoring and localized production. This structural change, driven by national security and economic resilience concerns, acts as a powerful tailwind for India's Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector. It creates an urgent need and strategic imperative to develop domestic manufacturing capabilities, directly increasing demand for local equipment and materials providers.

forces.title: Low R&D investment hindering innovation in deep tech
forces.description: India's R&D investment, at approximately 0.7% of GDP, remains significantly below leading innovation economies (3-4%). This underinvestment creates a substantial impediment for deep technology and scientific innovation, which are crucial for developing advanced semiconductor equipment and materials. This deficiency limits the country's ability to create cutting-edge indigenous technologies and reduces the competitiveness of its offerings in a highly R&D-intensive sector, posing a long-term risk to growth and self-reliance.

forces.title: Limited patient capital for deep tech and cutting-edge startups
forces.description: The availability of patient capital for frontier bets and deep tech startups is limited in India, with few investors funding the 10-15 year commercialization cycles typical of scientific innovation. This scarcity of long-term investment is a significant headwind for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector, as the development of advanced machinery and novel materials requires substantial, sustained funding over extended periods. It restricts the emergence and growth of indigenous companies in this capital-intensive segment.

forces.title: Skill imbalance in AI and product-engineering a bottleneck
forces.description: India faces an imbalance in advanced skills, particularly in AI, product-led engineering, and frontier R&D, leading to a shortage of top-tier talent. This skill gap is a headwind for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector because the design, development, and operation of sophisticated semiconductor manufacturing equipment and the formulation of advanced materials require highly specialized engineering and scientific expertise. Addressing this imbalance is crucial for building indigenous capabilities and competitiveness.

forces.title: India's low market share in high-growth semiconductor sector
forces.description: Despite the global semiconductor sector exhibiting high growth (10-20% CAGR) and attractive valuation multiples (14-15x EV), India's market share in this segment is currently very low. The Indian tech industry remains heavily concentrated in IT-enabled services. This underrepresentation in a strategically critical and rapidly expanding sector like semiconductors poses a key risk of missing out on significant future value creation and perpetuating import dependence for advanced electronic components.

forces.title: 100% FDI in ESDM attracting investment in wafer fabrication
forces.description: India's policy allowing 100% FDI under the automatic route in the Electronics System Design & Manufacturing (ESDM) sector is a significant tailwind. It actively encourages investments from OEMs and IDMs, with "semiconductor wafer fabrication" explicitly highlighted as a key area of interest. This open investment framework directly facilitates the establishment and expansion of chip manufacturing facilities, thereby driving substantial demand for advanced semiconductor equipment and materials from foreign and domestic players.

viewpoints.title: India's Semiconductor Mission poised for vertical integration and reduced import reliance
viewpoints.description: KPMG views India's Semiconductor Mission as a cornerstone policy initiative with a long-term commitment to indigenizing semiconductor components. Approved investments in fabrication plants and Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) facilities are expected to significantly reduce India's near-total import dependence on semiconductors. This strategic bet is anticipated to create a foundation for a more vertically integrated electronics ecosystem within India, fostering growth for semiconductor equipment and materials suppliers.

viewpoints.title: India's electronics sector faces "incentive-led plateau" risk
viewpoints.description: KPMG highlights a critical risk for India's electronics manufacturing, including its nascent semiconductor industry: over-reliance on production-linked incentives (PLI). While PLI schemes build capacity, they don't inherently create competitiveness. If cost competitiveness remains dependent on these disbursements rather than organic productivity and ecosystem advantages, the sector faces a "viability cliff" as incentives taper. A shift towards capability incentives, rewarding value-add and design integration, is crucial to avoid this plateau.

viewpoints.title: 2026 marks landmark year for India’s semiconductor industry
viewpoints.description: The Union IT Minister, Mr. Ashwini Vaishnaw, has declared 2026 a landmark year for India's semiconductor industry, with four semiconductor units poised to commence commercial production. This positive outlook is underpinned by the expansion of the India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 and the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS), bolstered by a US$ 4.5 billion outlay aimed at strengthening domestic supply chains for chips and components. This signifies a strong trajectory for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector.

viewpoints.title: India poised to launch first domestically produced semiconductor chip by 2025
viewpoints.description: IBEF reports that India plans to launch its first domestically produced semiconductor chip by the end of 2025, utilizing 28 to 90 nanometer technology. This ambitious goal is supported by the approval of a sixth semiconductor manufacturing facility (HCL and Foxconn JV) and the ongoing development of six chip fabrication units. This move, emphasizing indigenous intellectual property and chip design, signals a strong positive trajectory for the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector by creating local demand for fabrication technologies.

viewpoints.title: India must invest in semiconductors as a "Big Bet"
viewpoints.description: BCG identifies Semiconductors as a critical "Big Bet" for India to drive disproportionate value creation in the next decade, moving beyond its strength in IT Consulting and Services. This segment, characterized by being capital intensive, IP-led, R&D-driven, and ecosystem-dependent, requires significant risk capital, R&D intensity, public-private coordination, and long-term policy continuity. This strategic prioritization is crucial for fostering a robust domestic semiconductor ecosystem, which directly benefits the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector.

viewpoints.title: India must build semiconductor capabilities alongside IT services growth
viewpoints.description: NASSCOM emphasizes that India's sustained global relevance necessitates a dual strategy: strengthening its core IT services, GCC, and BPO leadership while simultaneously building robust capabilities in emerging areas like AI, software, platforms, semiconductors, and deep tech. This requires increased R&D investments and greater risk capital for startups, transforming engineers into inventors. For the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials sector, this implies a strategic imperative for focused development and investment to support a broader, technologically advanced Indian tech landscape.

viewpoints.title: India's minimal semiconductor presence creates "Burning Platform" challenge
viewpoints.description: BCG warns that India's minimal presence in high-growth, R&D-intensive sectors like semiconductors presents a "Burning Platform" challenge. Despite a strong footprint in IT services, India is significantly underrepresented in segments defining the future of global tech. This lack of participation in critical sectors, including Semiconductor Equipment & Materials, means India risks missing out on future value creation and global competitiveness if it does not strategically invest and build capabilities in these areas.

demand_drivers.driver: Strong demand across diverse electronic product categories
demand_drivers.description: Growing demand for electronic products in IT, office automation, telecom, consumer electronics, aviation, aerospace, defense, solar PV, nano electronics, and medical electronics drives the overall ESDM market.
Government initiatives and policies promoting electronics manufacturing and design contribute to market expansion.
The ongoing trend of digitalization across sectors boosts the need for electronic systems and components.

market_sizing.methodology: Valuation of the Electronics System Design & Manufacturing (ESDM) industry, which includes electronic hardware products and components, IT, office automation, telecom, consumer electronics, aviation, aerospace, defense, solar PV, nano electronics, medical electronics, as well as design-related activities like product design, chip design, VLSI, board design, and embedded systems.

demand_drivers.driver: India's overall electronics manufacturing growth target
demand_drivers.description: India's electronics industry is targeting a manufacturing output of Rs. 43,10,000 crore (US$ 500 billion) by FY30, requiring a fivefold increase in production. This ambitious target creates significant demand for upstream components, including semiconductors, and therefore for semiconductor equipment and materials.

market_sizing.methodology: India's overall electronics industry target for manufacturing output. No explicit market size for IN080402 is given, but this ambitious target implies massive growth for upstream suppliers like semiconductor equipment and materials.

demand_drivers.description: A dedicated outlay of Rs. 8,000 crore (US$ 0.90 billion) for FY27 under ISM 2.0 explicitly focuses on developing domestic capabilities in semiconductor equipment and materials.

Over US$ 15 billion in total investment for three semiconductor plants, including OSAT and foundry facilities by Tata Electronics and Intel, directly translates to demand for fabrication machinery and materials.
ECMS attracting investments far exceeding targets indicates a broader push for domestic component manufacturing, indirectly supporting upstream semiconductor material demand.

new_opportunities.description: ISM 2.0's focus on advancing full-stack Indian IP and strengthening supply chains through industry-led research creates opportunities for indigenous development and supply of semiconductor equipment and materials.
new_opportunities.opportunity: Establishing full-stack Indian IP in semiconductors

market_sizing.methodology: Analysis of government and private investment in semiconductor manufacturing and related schemes, directly indicating future demand for equipment and materials.

demand_drivers.description: Electronics production surged from US$21.43 billion in 2014-15 to US$127 billion in 2024-25. This six-fold increase directly fuels demand for components, especially semiconductors, and therefore for semiconductor equipment and materials.

India aims for electronics exports to reach US$120 billion by FY26 (up from US$15 billion in FY22), positioning electronics among the top 2-3 export categories. This export-oriented growth strategy requires a robust domestic manufacturing base for chips, equipment, and materials.
India became the top smartphone exporter to the US in Q2 FY26. The substantial increase in smartphone production for both domestic and export markets is a major driver for semiconductor demand.

market_sizing.methodology: Growth in overall electronics production and export targets, particularly for smartphones, necessitating increased semiconductor manufacturing. No explicit market size for IN080402, but strong demand drivers identified.

demand_drivers.description: The Indian IT Hardware market is projected to grow from US$21.17 billion in 2025 to US$31.39 billion in 2031 at a CAGR of 6.78%. This growth in devices like computers, servers, and peripherals directly increases the demand for semiconductors, thus indirectly benefiting the semiconductor equipment and materials sector.

market_sizing.methodology: Forecasted growth of the IT Hardware market. No explicit market size for IN080402, but the expansion of IT Hardware necessitates increased demand for semiconductors and their manufacturing inputs.

demand_drivers.description: Server expenditure is anticipated to surge by 36.9% YoY in 2026, driven by increasing data processing needs and cloud infrastructure expansion. This directly boosts demand for high-performance processors and memory, which are reliant on advanced semiconductor equipment and materials.

Data center spending is projected to climb 31.7% in 2026, exceeding US$650 billion. The expansion and modernization of data centers globally necessitate significant investment in underlying semiconductor technologies, driving demand for the IN080402 sector.

market_sizing.methodology: Global IT expenditure forecasts, specifically server and data center spending, indicating underlying demand for advanced semiconductor components. No explicit market size for IN080402, but strong demand drivers identified.

demand_drivers.driver: Doubled allocation for Modified Semiconductor and Display Manufacturing Programme
demand_drivers.description: The allocation nearly doubled to Rs. 8,000 crore (US$0.90 billion), directly boosting efforts in semiconductor and display manufacturing, which requires extensive equipment and materials.

demand_drivers.driver: ISM 2.0 focus on domestic equipment and materials capabilities
demand_drivers.description: ISM 2.0's stated aim to develop domestic capabilities in semiconductor equipment and materials, advance full-stack Indian IP, and strengthen supply chains, directly creates and supports market demand for IN080402.

new_opportunities.description: ISM 2.0 specifically promotes advancing full-stack Indian IP, indicating a future where indigenous solutions for equipment and materials may be prioritized.
new_opportunities.opportunity: Advancing full-stack Indian IP in semiconductors

market_sizing.methodology: Government allocations and programmatic goals specifically targeting semiconductor and display manufacturing, and domestic capabilities for equipment and materials. No explicit market size for IN080402, but strong demand drivers identified.

demand_drivers.description: The addressable market for Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) in handset manufacturing is projected to reach US$140-150 billion by 2025. This massive scale of domestic production for smartphones (including US$30 billion in exports) directly drives significant demand for semiconductor components, and consequently, the equipment and materials required for their fabrication.

market_sizing.methodology: Forecasted market for OEMs in handset manufacturing indicates the scale of the electronics assembly market. No explicit market size for IN080402, but strong demand drivers identified.

demand_drivers.driver: General growth of the global semiconductor market
demand_drivers.description: The global semiconductor market, estimated at $0.8-1 trillion, is growing at a strong rate (10-20% CAGR for 2024-29). This sustained expansion drives the need for new and upgraded manufacturing facilities, thus generating significant demand for semiconductor equipment and materials.

pnl_drivers.description: Semiconductors command high EV multiples of 14-15x, indicating strong profitability and investor confidence in the sector. This attractive financial performance supports investment in high-cost equipment and R&D for materials.

market_sizing.methodology: Global market size estimate for the semiconductor industry, which directly influences demand for semiconductor equipment and materials. The global market size is stated as $0.8-1T, with the lower end chosen for this entry. Includes Semiconductors (IG0804) which drives demand for IN080402.
